blocks.text: A 22-year-old gymnast has skin that stretches several centimetres, joints that bend beyond normal range, and wounds that heal as wide, thin scars. Her collagen is built wrongly, and understanding why requires knowing how connective tissue cells make and assemble it.

blocks.markdown: Connective tissue is defined less by its cells than by its **extracellular matrix (ECM)**: fibres plus a hydrated **ground substance** of glycosaminoglycans and proteoglycans that fills space and resists compression. **Fibroblasts** are the principal cells that make collagen, elastic fibre components and ground substance. Other cells include **macrophages** (phagocytosis, antigen processing), **mast cells** (granules with histamine and heparin, stain metachromatically, role in allergy), **plasma cells** (antibody secretion), and **adipocytes** (fat storage).

blocks.title: Core terms
blocks.text: Loose connective tissue has abundant ground substance and sparse fibres. Dense connective tissue has abundant collagen and little ground substance: in dense regular tissue the bundles are parallel; in dense irregular tissue they are interwoven in many planes. Collagen provides tensile strength; elastic fibres (elastin on a fibrillin scaffold) allow recoil.

rows: Sparse, loosely woven collagen and elastic fibres
Packing, diffusion, support of vessels and nerves
Lamina propria, around vessels, beneath epithelia
Parallel collagen bundles with rows of fibroblasts
blocks.caption: Common connective tissue types

blocks.title: Naming a tissue from its histology
blocks.prompt: A section shows thick pink collagen bundles running parallel in a tightly packed array with rows of flattened fibroblast nuclei between them, from a structure joining muscle to bone. Which tissue is this?

steps.text: Thick eosinophilic collagen bundles with scant ground substance mean dense connective tissue.
The bundles are parallel with rows of fibroblasts, so the fibre direction is single-axis: dense regular.
A structure linking muscle to bone is a tendon, which resists unidirectional pull.

blocks.answer: Dense regular connective tissue of a tendon.

blocks.markdown: **Collagen types.** Type I is the most abundant (skin, tendon, bone, dentin); type II forms hyaline and elastic cartilage; type III forms reticular fibres (vessel walls, hollow organs, lymphoid organs); type IV forms the basal lamina. Collagen's repeating unit is Gly-X-Y, where X and Y are often proline and hydroxyproline, and every third residue must be glycine for the chains to pack into a tight triple helix.

**Collagen biosynthesis.** (1) Pre-pro-alpha chains are translated into the rough endoplasmic reticulum, and the signal peptide is removed. (2) Selected proline and lysine residues are hydroxylated by prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases, enzymes that require **vitamin C** (ascorbate) as a cofactor; hydroxyproline stabilises the helix, and some hydroxylysine is glycosylated. (3) Three chains assemble into a **procollagen triple helix** with propeptides at both ends. (4) Procollagen is transported through the Golgi and secreted by exocytosis. (5) Extracellular **procollagen peptidases** cleave the N- and C-terminal propeptides to give tropocollagen. (6) Tropocollagen self-assembles into fibrils, which are covalently cross-linked by **lysyl oxidase** (a copper-dependent enzyme), then into fibres and bundles.

rows: Unstable helix, poor cross-linking; bleeding gums, perifollicular haemorrhage, poor wound healing
Mutations in type I collagen genes, often a glycine substitution that disrupts the triple helix, or reduced type I collagen
Abnormal collagen structure or processing, for example type V collagen or procollagen peptidase defects in some forms, type III collagen in vascular type
Hyperextensible skin, joint hypermobility, fragile vessels or skin depending on type
blocks.caption: Collagen disorders linked to specific steps

blocks.title: Linking a defect to the tissue finding
blocks.prompt: A mutation replaces a glycine in a type I collagen chain with a bulkier amino acid. Explain the effect on bone.

steps.text: Glycine at every third position lets the three chains pack tightly into the triple helix.
A bulkier residue distorts the helix, so the assembled collagen is abnormal and degraded or secreted in faulty form.
Bone matrix is mostly type I collagen with mineral deposited on it, so a weak collagen scaffold gives brittle, fracture-prone bone.

blocks.answer: Glycine substitution disrupts the triple helix, weakening type I collagen and causing brittle bone (osteogenesis imperfecta).

blocks.markdown: **Using a scale bar.** Actual size = (measured object / measured scale bar) x labelled bar length. For example, a bar labelled 100 nm measuring 20 mm and a fibril 10 mm wide gives $10/20 \times 100 = 50$ nm.

items: Fibroblasts make collagen, elastic fibres and ground substance.
Dense regular tissue (parallel bundles) suits tendons and ligaments; dense irregular (interwoven bundles) suits dermis and capsules.
Collagen synthesis: rER translation, hydroxylation (vitamin C), triple helix, secretion, peptidase cleavage, cross-linking.

blocks.title: Common pitfall
blocks.text: Dense regular and dense irregular tissue are both collagen-rich: the difference is fibre orientation, not density. Also, collagen cannot form properly without vitamin C, so scurvy is a failure of collagen biosynthesis, not of collagen gene sequence.

points: The ECM (fibres plus ground substance) defines connective tissue, and fibroblasts are its principal synthesising cells.
Dense regular tissue has parallel bundles (tendon, ligament); dense irregular has interwoven bundles (dermis, capsules).

Collagen biosynthesis involves rER translation, vitamin C-dependent hydroxylation, triple helix formation, secretion, procollagen peptidase cleavage and cross-linking; defects explain scurvy, osteogenesis imperfecta and Ehlers-Danlos syndromes.

questions.stem: A section of reticular dermis shows thick collagen bundles cut in several planes, interwoven, with few cells and little ground substance. Which tissue is this and why?

options.text: Dense irregular connective tissue, because the bundles run in many directions
Dense regular connective tissue, because the bundles are collagen-rich
Loose connective tissue, because cells are few
Reticular tissue, because type III collagen forms thick bundles

questions.correctOptionText: Dense irregular connective tissue, because the bundles run in many directions

distractorRationale.b: Both dense types are collagen-rich; orientation distinguishes them.
distractorRationale.c: Loose tissue has abundant ground substance and sparse fibres.
distractorRationale.d: Reticular fibres are thin type III fibres, not thick bundles.

questions.explanation: The key discriminator is fibre orientation. Interwoven bundles resist stress from many directions, as in the dermis, whereas parallel bundles indicate dense regular tissue.

questions.stem: Near a small venule in the lamina propria, a round cell contains many coarse granules that stain metachromatically with toluidine blue and release histamine on allergen exposure. Which cell is this?

options.text: Mast cell
Plasma cell
Fibroblast
Adipocyte

distractorRationale.b: Plasma cells secrete antibody and have basophilic cytoplasm.
distractorRationale.c: Fibroblasts synthesise matrix and have spindle shape.

questions.explanation: Mast cells contain heparin and histamine granules that stain metachromatically and degranulate in allergic responses. They are a resident cell of loose connective tissue.

questions.stem: A man on a diet lacking fresh fruit and vegetables for months develops bleeding gums and perifollicular haemorrhages, and an old scar reopens. Which step of collagen synthesis is most directly impaired?

options.text: Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in the rough endoplasmic reticulum
Cleavage of propeptides by procollagen peptidase outside the cell
Translation of pre-pro-alpha chains on free ribosomes
Secretion of procollagen from the nucleus

questions.correctOptionText: Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in the rough endoplasmic reticulum

distractorRationale.a: Correct: vitamin C is the cofactor for hydroxylases.
distractorRationale.b: Peptidases do not require vitamin C.
distractorRationale.c: Translation is intact in scurvy; chains are made on the rER.
distractorRationale.d: Procollagen is secreted via the Golgi, not from the nucleus.

questions.explanation: Vitamin C deficiency is scurvy; prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases need ascorbate, so under-hydroxylated chains form unstable helices and weak fibrils. This explains fragile vessels and poor healing.

questions.stem: On an electron micrograph of tendon, a scale bar labelled 200 nm measures 25 mm. A collagen fibril measures 10 mm across. Calculate the fibril diameter in nanometres.
questions.explanation: True size = (10 / 25) x 200 = 80 nanometres, within the range expected for collagen fibrils. The scale bar supplies the conversion between image and real size.

questions.stem: Outline the steps of collagen synthesis from gene to mature fibril and explain why a defect at one step produces connective tissue disease.
markingGuide: Pre-pro-alpha chains are synthesised into the rough ER by fibroblasts.
Proline and lysine hydroxylation requires vitamin C.
Three chains form the procollagen triple helix (glycine every third residue).
Procollagen is secreted via the Golgi; extracellular peptidases cleave propeptides to tropocollagen.
Tropocollagen assembles into fibrils cross-linked by lysyl oxidase.
A defect weakens tensile strength, with a named example such as scurvy, osteogenesis imperfecta or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome linked to a specific step.
questions.explanation: A full answer follows the sequence and links one disorder to a specific step. Collagen is the main tensile element, so errors weaken skin, bone, vessels or ligaments.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old has had five fractures after minor falls and has blue-tinged sclerae. A mutation in the gene for the most abundant collagen of bone is suspected. Which collagen is affected?

options.text: Type I
Type II
Type III
Type IV

distractorRationale.a: Correct: type I is the major collagen of bone, skin and tendon.
distractorRationale.d: Type IV forms the basal lamina.

questions.explanation: Osteogenesis imperfecta results from defects in type I collagen, the major organic component of bone matrix. The thin sclera shows the underlying choroid, giving the blue tinge.

questions.stem: A light micrograph of dermis has a scale bar labelled 50 micrometres that measures 20 mm. A collagen bundle measures 24 mm across. Calculate the bundle width in micrometres.
questions.explanation: True width = (24 / 20) x 50 = 60 micrometres. Such thick bundles are typical of dense connective tissue.

questions.stem: Describe the cells and matrix of loose connective tissue and explain how these features support its function.
markingGuide: Fibroblasts synthesise matrix; other cells include macrophages, mast cells, plasma cells and adipocytes.
Abundant hydrated ground substance and sparse collagen and elastic fibres.
The loose arrangement permits diffusion, packing and support around vessels, nerves and epithelia.
questions.explanation: A good answer links the abundant ground substance to diffusion and the sparse fibres to flexibility. Distinguish cells from extracellular matrix.

questions.stem: Which pairing of tissue, location and functional reason is correct?

options.text: Dense regular connective tissue in a ligament, because tension acts along one axis
Dense irregular connective tissue in a tendon, because tension acts along many axes
Dense regular connective tissue in the dermis, because tension acts along one axis
Loose connective tissue in an organ capsule, because it resists multidirectional stress

questions.correctOptionText: Dense regular connective tissue in a ligament, because tension acts along one axis

distractorRationale.d: Capsules are dense irregular; loose tissue is not load-bearing.

questions.explanation: Parallel bundles match unidirectional tension in tendons and ligaments, while interwoven bundles suit dermis and capsules. Matching tissue to load direction is the key skill.

questions.stem: Procollagen leaves the fibroblast and is converted to tropocollagen. Where and by what action does this conversion occur?

options.text: Extracellularly, by procollagen peptidases removing the terminal propeptides
In the rough ER, by hydroxylases removing the signal peptide
In the nucleus, by splicing out introns
In lysosomes, by acid hydrolases

questions.correctOptionText: Extracellularly, by procollagen peptidases removing the terminal propeptides

distractorRationale.b: Hydroxylases modify residues; signal peptide removal is separate and earlier.
distractorRationale.d: Lysosomes degrade material and do not process procollagen.

questions.explanation: Propeptides keep procollagen soluble inside the cell; cleaving them outside the cell allows tropocollagen to assemble into fibrils. Defective cleavage gives disorganised fibrils as in some Ehlers-Danlos forms.

questions.stem: Compare scurvy and osteogenesis imperfecta as disorders of collagen, identifying the step of synthesis affected in each and the resulting tissue findings.
markingGuide: Scurvy: lack of vitamin C impairs hydroxylation of proline and lysine.
Unstable helix and poor cross-linking cause fragile vessels, bleeding gums and poor healing.
Osteogenesis imperfecta: type I collagen gene mutation, often glycine substitution disrupting the triple helix.
Weak type I collagen causes brittle bones and blue sclerae.
Both reduce tensile integrity of collagen but by different mechanisms: acquired cofactor deficiency versus inherited structural defect.
questions.explanation: Scurvy is a nutritional defect in a post-translational step, whereas osteogenesis imperfecta is an inherited defect in the chain itself. Both end in a weak collagen scaffold.

questions.stem: Which cell is the principal producer of collagen and ground substance in connective tissue?

options.text: Fibroblast
Macrophage
Mast cell
Plasma cell

questions.explanation: Fibroblasts are the main synthetic cells of connective tissue and also drive repair. The other cells have defence-related roles.
